title: Devil Dice
subtitle: Turning the floor into a puzzle
summary: Devil Dice is Shift's PlayStation puzzle game, first released in Japan as XI on 18 June 1998. A small devil runs across a field of oversized dice, climbing on top to roll them into useful positions. Matching numbers makes groups sink and disappear, but reaching the correct face requires thinking about how each die will turn along the way. body: Devil Dice is Shift's PlayStation puzzle game, first released in Japan as XI on 18 June 1998. A small devil runs across a field of oversized dice, climbing on top to roll them into useful positions. Matching numbers makes groups sink and disappear, but reaching the correct face requires thinking about how each die will turn along the way. The board is both a moving platform and the material of the puzzle. That connection lets a simple-looking field produce increasingly difficult decisions about position, orientation and the space available for the next move.

A group must contain at least as many matching dice as the number showing on their upper faces. Two twos can begin a clear, while sixes require a larger gathering. The dice sink gradually, leaving a short opportunity to add more matching pieces and extend the chain. Running in a direction rolls the die beneath the devil, exposing another face and changing where he stands. The useful move therefore has two consequences at once: it prepares a number and carries the player towards, or away from, the next part of the arrangement.

Devil Dice emerged from Sony's Game Yarōze initiative, which invited proposals that could become commercial PlayStation games. Lead designer Yuichi Sugiyama and programmer Shuichi Yano later described that route into development, distinguishing it from the similarly named Net Yaroze programme. The finished game combined solitary puzzle solving with competitive modes, including play for five people through a multitap. Critics welcomed the idea while noting its difficulty. Kemmei Adachi composed the music, and later related games carried the rolling-dice concept to other hardware, including the PlayStation 2 follow-up Bombastic.

From an open call to the living room
